# The Gold Watch

Rollo and Marcus drove across the city arguing about drug laws in foreign countries and what they called fast food overseas. Neither point was settled by the time they reached the apartment block. In the corridor outside their target's flat they fell to bickering about whether a foot massage was worth killing a man over, and Marcus, who had strong views on the matter, recited a passage of scripture before they kicked in the door and shot young Tobin for double-crossing their employer Otis. They recovered the briefcase. A fourth man hidden in the bathroom emptied a revolver at them from point-blank range without landing a single round, which Marcus called divine intervention. In the car afterwards, Rollo's gun went off and blew the head off their passenger Del. Marcus drove the bloodied car to his friend Warren's house, where a fixer named Winston directed the cleanup and handed the men fresh clothes. Over breakfast in a coffee shop, two small-time robbers decided on the spot to hold up the diner they were sitting in. Marcus talked the robber down mid-holdup, handed over his own wallet, kept the briefcase, and let the couple walk out. The two hitmen delivered the briefcase to Otis at his bar, where Otis was paying the ageing boxer Denny to take a dive in the fifth.

---

Rollo bought heroin from his dealer Kip and shot up before his night out. He took Otis's wife Nadia to a themed diner where they won the dance contest. Nadia snorted Rollo's heroin, overdosed, and was revived by an adrenaline shot to the heart on the dealer's living-room floor.

---

Years earlier, a returning prisoner of war had delivered to a young boy the gold watch his father kept hidden through years of captivity.

Denny double-crossed Otis, won the fight and killed his opponent in the ring, then escaped in a taxi. Hiding in a motel with his girlfriend Marielle, Denny discovered she had left his father's watch behind in his flat. He returned for the watch and shot Rollo dead with a submachine gun left on the kitchen counter. Denny and Otis collided in the street, crashed, and were taken prisoner in the basement of a pawnshop. Denny broke free, came back with a sword from the shop wall while one of their captors was raping Otis, and Otis declared them square on condition Denny leaves town. Denny collected Marielle and rode out of the city on a motorcycle taken from the pawnshop.

The robbery collapsed within a minute. Sirens clawed through the morning air before Mr. Ash had even reached the car, and then he was shooting, the windshield of a patrol cruiser starring white and the vehicle slewing into a lamppost. Mr. Elm rode shotgun, hunched and pale, and Ash floored it through a curtain of gunfire.

Later—much later, in a room that smelled of industrial solvent and old coffee—Danny Roarke had stood in front of a one-way mirror and told a story about a drug bust in a public toilet until his handler Pruitt stopped correcting him. "Again," Pruitt said. "You're not reciting, you're remembering." Danny told it four more times, changing the weather, changing the color of the tiles, until the anecdote sat in his mouth like something he had lived. He performed it for Bram and his son Cal and the silent Mr. Ash, and Bram nodded once and said, "Mr. Elm," and that was that.

Now Elm was bleeding. Fleeing on foot after the car died, he had hijacked a sedan at a junction and the terrified driver had shot him in the stomach before Elm put two rounds into the man's chest. Ash dragged him back to the replacement vehicle, drove howling through back streets to the warehouse rendezvous, and cradled him against his chest on the oil-stained concrete, swearing he was not going to die.

Ren Vasco had walked out of prison on a Tuesday morning carrying a cardboard box of letters he never intended to read. He reported to Bram and Cal that afternoon. They owed him for the years he had kept his mouth shut, and they knew it, and the knowing sat between them at breakfast like a fourth person at the table. The crew argued about what a pop song was really about—Cal insisted it was about a girl, Bram said it was about money—and whether waitresses deserved a tip when the coffee was cold. Ren said nothing. He ate his eggs.

Mr. Birch arrived at the warehouse, took one look at the blood and the shouting, and said the job was a setup. There was an informer inside it. He would not say who. He took the diamonds and hid them outside the building in a drainpipe, came back empty-handed, and leaned against the loading bay door with his arms folded.

Bram had handed out the tree aliases months ago, standing at the head of that same breakfast table like a foreman assigning shifts. Mr. Birch had objected to being Mr. Birch. "Birch is a woman's name," he said, and Bram looked at him with absolutely no expression and said, "No, it isn't," and that was the end of it.

Mr. Cedar strolled in whistling, popped the boot of his car, and produced a kidnapped patrolman named Doyle, bound and gagged and wide-eyed with terror. Cedar dumped him on the warehouse floor like a man unpacking groceries. Left alone with the bound officer, Cedar turned on a radio—some oldie, strings and saxophone—and danced to it, loose-limbed and grinning, before he cut off Doyle's ear with a folding knife and doused him in petrol from a jerrican he had brought for the purpose.

Mr. Elm shot Mr. Cedar dead from the floor where he lay. The bullet took Cedar in the throat and he dropped the jerrican and went down hard, his heels drumming. Elm looked at Doyle and said, "I'm a cop. The police are waiting outside for Bram. You're going to be all right."

Cal returned, listened to Elm's account of what Cedar had done, looked at the body, looked at the petrol, looked at Doyle, and shot the patrolman dead himself. The sound was enormous in the warehouse.

Bram arrived last. He walked in calm, surveyed the scene, and named Mr. Elm as the informer. He said it the way he said everything, as though the words had already been true for some time. Mr. Ash refused to believe him. Ash turned his gun on Bram, and Bram turned his on Ash, and Cal drew his, and the three-way standoff lasted perhaps four seconds before everyone fired.

Bram and Cal went down. Ash went down. Only Ash and Elm were still breathing.

Elm confessed. He said it plainly: he was a police officer, his name was Danny Roarke, and it was over. Ash looked at him with something that might have been grief and shot him in the chest. The warehouse doors burst open and the police stormed in, and Ash was cut down in a line of fire that went on and on, the radio still playing, the saxophone thinning to nothing above the noise.

Aaron opens his eyes and there is a fist of muscle in his chest where there was nothing. A nurse holds a clipboard. He is alive. He has not been alive in months. Something belongs to him that did not belong to him.

Wes Tarrow crouches behind the backstop showing a boy how to turn his hips. The boys listen. Wes has a stillness about him that makes them listen. At home Nita watches him pray and does not pray with him. She watches his hands. She watches the way his jaw sets when the praying is done.

Lena Ward sits on the tile floor of her bathroom with a mirror and a rolled bill and a calm that frightens her. She does it well. She has done it well. The suburban house around her is immaculate and empty and she is destroying it methodically, starting with herself.

Della stands in Aaron's hospital room with paperwork and a thermos and the argument they have been having for years compressed into a single request. His sperm is frozen. She wants a child. He is dying. She says the word *before* and he hears it as a threat.

Aaron stands at the edge of a public pool. A woman swims laps. He has followed her here. He has paid someone to find her. He does not know what he will say. She climbs out and he says something about the chlorine and she laughs and they go to a diner and then to her house and then to a place that has no name.

Wes walks into a police station. He sits in a chair. He says the words. They put him in a room. He is calm. He has been calm since he turned the truck around and then did not turn the truck around. He is calm the way a man is calm when he has decided everything.

A doctor stands in front of Aaron and says the word *weeks*. Aaron hears the word the way you hear a door closing in another room. Della is not there. The doctor's mouth moves and Aaron watches it and thinks about numbers, about the clean logic of limits approaching zero.

Lena sets the table for four. Doug will be home. The girls are playing in the yard. She puts out the good plates. She is happy in a way she does not trust because she has not been happy in a long time and happiness has always been the thing that comes right before.

Aaron tells Lena. He says the word *donor* and the word *husband* and the word *heart* and she goes white and throws a glass and throws him out and the door slams and the street is dark. She calls. She says come back. He goes back.

Wes's truck crosses an intersection. There are people in the crosswalk. The truck does not stop. The truck stops. The truck does not stop.

Aaron sits in an office and hands a photograph to a man and the man takes the photograph and Aaron says *widow* and the man nods. Aaron cannot stop thinking about the fist of muscle in his chest. Whose it was. What it remembers.

Aaron tells Della he is leaving. He tells her he does not want the child. She is holding a cup of coffee and she does not put it down. She holds it and the coffee goes cold in her hands.

A doctor stands in front of Lena. He says the words. She hears none of them. She hears the word *all* and the word *three* and then she is in a hallway and the hallway is very long and very bright and she is alone in it.

Wes walks out of a gate. Nita is not there. No one is there. He takes a bus to a town whose name he does not learn. He works at a motel. He makes the beds. He does not pray.

Lena says the word *kill*. She says it plainly. Aaron listens. He buys a gun.

Aaron stands in a motel room with the gun. Wes is there. Wes is always there. Aaron pulls the trigger and Wes falls and Aaron tells him to run and Wes does not run.

Wes follows them. He finds them. He asks Aaron to finish it. Aaron puts the gun against his own head.

Lena and Wes drive Aaron to a hospital. The heart fails. Wes goes home to Nita. Lena goes home alone. She is pregnant. She does not know what she is carrying.

# Bluebell

The reporter Nash stood at the gate of Silvermount and watched workmen shovel a child's sled into a furnace. The name BLUEBELL was painted on its runner in flaking red. He had been sent to find out what the word meant, the word Emmett Rusk had died with, and he was no closer now than when he'd started.

He had read Barrow's memoir first. The banker described how, in a mining boarding house out west, Emmett's mother had signed her son over to him after a defaulted lodger's mine deed made the family rich. The boy had driven his sled into Barrow's stomach, and been taken east anyway. Barrow called it the first proof of the boy's stubbornness. He did not mention the sled's name.

Nash interviewed Marsh next, who had been installed as manager when Emmett took control of his fortune on his twenty-fifth birthday and chose to run the failing Clarion. Emmett had printed a signed statement of principles on the front page, hired away the entire staff of the rival paper, and thrown a party with a brass band and a chorus line. Marsh said Emmett believed a newspaper was a weapon. He said it without admiration.

Devlin, Emmett's friend, told Nash about the buying trip abroad. Emmett returned engaged to Adele, the governor's niece. The marriage cooled into silence behind separate newspapers at the breakfast table. Then Emmett met the shopgirl Nora Kell on the street with mud on his coat and started visiting her rooms in secret. Devlin had watched it happen. He had asked to be transferred to another city after Emmett lost the governor's race, when the party boss Halloran brought Adele to Nora's rooms and threatened exposure and Emmett refused to withdraw. The marriage collapsed. Devlin said Emmett did not know how to lose anything gracefully.

Nash found Nora in a seaside nightclub, drunk. She would not talk. He pieced together the rest from the butler Colm and from what he could read in the ruins of Silvermount.

Emmett had married Nora and forced her into an opera career for which she had no voice. Her debut was a humiliation. Devlin, drunk, began the savage review. Emmett finished it, printed it, and fired him for it. Nora swallowed poison rather than sing again, and Emmett finally let her stop. He shut her away in the half-finished palace he called Silvermount, where she worked jigsaw puzzles in the vast empty hall. After a joyless beach picnic and a quarrel, she packed and left him.

Colm showed Nash the bedroom Emmett had wrecked after Nora's departure. In the debris Nash found a glass snow globe. Colm said Emmett had murmured "Bluebell" and carried it past the endless mirrors.

Nash visited the newsreel archive. The obituary recapped Emmett's public life and closed without explaining his last word.

He went back to the nightclub. Nora was still drunk. She told him to leave. He left.

Standing at the gate now, watching the sled burn, Nash thought about the boy who had driven that sled into Barrow's stomach. He thought about the mother who had signed her son away and the son who had spent his life signing things himself—principles, reviews, marriage licenses. No single word explains a life. The sled had a name. The man who owned it had died with that name on his lips, and the name had meant something once, something before the money, before the newspaper, before the opera, before the poison and the palace and the mirrors.

The fire consumed the last of the wood. Nash turned and walked away from Silvermount. He had his story. It was that there was no story. There was only a boy and a sled and a word, and a life that had used everything up except that.

He and his crew dressed as devout pilgrims, heads bowed, prayer beads clicking in their fingers, and walked into the diamond house in the northern port as though they had come to pray. They walked out with a stone the size of a pigeon's egg. Across the water, his cousin Marv sent word: bring it straight over, no stops, no fuss.

But Solly never could resist a detour. Grigor the Nail found him first, told him about a bookmaker's in the city where the odds were sweet, and at the same time sent quiet word to the pawnbrokers Ike and Benno that a man with something valuable would be walking through those doors. Grigor had a way of setting plates spinning and watching which ones fell.

Meanwhile, the boxing promoters Halloway and Digby had troubles of their own. They sent their man Pretty Sam to buy a caravan from a camp of travellers, but a bare-knuckle fighter named Finn knocked Sam cold over the deal. That left Halloway without a fighter for the fixed bout they had promised the gang boss Coldstone. Desperate, Halloway put Finn in the fight and swore to Coldstone the man would go down in the fourth round.

Solly landed in the city, dropped the stone with the fence Hersch, and headed for the bookmaker's to lay money on the fight. He never saw Ike, Benno and Tulley coming. They bungled the robbery badly, took Solly's arm and his case, and were chased off by Grigor, who had been watching from across the street.

In the ring, Finn knocked his opponent out cold in the first round. Coldstone lost a fortune and took it out on Halloway with his fists.

Marv flew in that evening, found Solly's room empty, and hired the bounty hunter Ledge to track him down. But Grigor had already found Solly. He cut off the man's arm to pry the case open and found nothing inside. The stone was gone.

Ledge traced the pawnbrokers to a garage on the south side, shot their car to pieces, and took both them and the diamond. Coldstone, meanwhile, fed what was left of Solly to his pigs and told Halloway and Digby exactly what would happen to them if the second fight went wrong. They found Finn and told him to go down in the fourth. To make certain, Coldstone's men went to the travellers' camp and burned Finn's mother to death in her caravan.

Grigor intercepted Ledge's car on the road back, Ike and Benno still inside. The shootout was brief and ugly. Ledge, Grigor and Benno all fell. Tulley, who had been following at a distance, grabbed the dog and ran.

Finn stepped into the ring for the second fight. In the fourth round, instead of falling, he knocked his opponent out again. The travellers rose from the crowd with knives and guns and massacred Coldstone's men where they sat. Halloway and Digby found Coldstone himself hiding in a back room and shot him twice in the head. By morning the travellers had vanished like smoke.

The dog wandered the streets for two days before someone handed it in at a pet shop. It coughed up the diamond on the counter, a small wet stone gleaming on the newspaper. Halloway and Digby arrived that afternoon with blood still under their nails, and walked out holding it between them, wondering what in God's name they were supposed to do now.

Wilder sat in his study with the telephone receiver growing warm against his ear, listening to Emlyn's voice — calm, measured, almost lazy in its precision. *Four years*, Emlyn said. His wife had told him on the trip abroad. And he had never thought much of his friend's letters either. The line went dead and Wilder held the receiver a moment longer, as though the shape of the conversation might reverse itself if he waited.

He had rung Emlyn in a state, and Emlyn had come to his house that same evening, arriving with the unhurried air of a man keeping a long-standing appointment. They sat across from each other in the front room and Emlyn spoke as though he were reading from a ledger. Four years. The trip. Odile's confession. Everything filed and stored. Wilder understood now that the lunch, the dinners, the racquet-talk — all of it had been performed for his benefit, a stage built over a pit he had never thought to look into.

Only the night before, Odile had sat across from him in a bar and told him her marriage was over. Two years had passed since they had last seen each other regularly. She had spent the previous night, she said, confessing everything to her husband. She said it with a kind of wonder, as though the act of telling had emptied her of something she had not known she was carrying. And then she let slip, almost carelessly, that Emlyn had been publishing a writer whom Wilder represented — a writer the two men both quietly detested. The detail landed between them on the bar table like a coin neither of them reached for.

Before the bar, before the two-year silence, there had been the end of the rooms. Wilder and Odile decided the rented rooms had become a chore. They split the crockery with the solemnity of a minor divorce, each taking plates and cups that had never been used in any real kitchen. They surrendered the lease. The affair folded up like a tent and they walked away from it carrying nothing that mattered.

Before the end of the rooms, there had been dinners at the married couple's house. The two men discussed racquet games and schoolboy sport with a fluency that excluded Odile entirely. She would sit at her own table and watch her husband and her lover talk past her, and the strangeness of it was that neither man seemed to be performing. They simply had more to say to each other than either had to her.

And before the dinners, there had been the long restaurant lunch. Emlyn had drunk steadily through the afternoon, baiting Wilder about contemporary fiction with a kind of cheerful malice, never once mentioning what he had learned. Wilder had laughed and argued and felt the ground solid beneath him. He had not known he was standing on a trapdoor.

Before the lunch, Odile had returned from the trip abroad and gone straight to the rented rooms. She said nothing about the hotel, the letter held at the desk, the handwriting Emlyn recognised. The afternoon passed exactly as the others had. She had already confessed to her husband and was now keeping the secret from her lover, and the rooms went on as though nothing beneath them had shifted.

In the hotel abroad, Emlyn had asked about the letter. Odile had confessed. And Emlyn, with a gentleness that must have been worse than anger, had remarked that he had always been fonder of his friend than of his wife.

Before the trip, Odile had told Wilder she was carrying her husband's child. They had decided the rented rooms would go on exactly as before, and they had, for a while, because neither of them could think of a reason to stop.

Before the child, before the confession, there had been the rooms themselves — the quiet district, the linen, the plates, the small household they had built for an affair that needed a house to feel real.

And before the rooms, before any of it, there had been a party at the house of Wilder's closest friend. He had led Odile upstairs and told her how lovely she was while the other guests drank below. She had listened. That was the beginning.

# Slaughterhouse

He has come unstuck in time. Or that is what he tells himself. The optometrist's daughter presses a glass of water into his hand and says nothing. Somewhere a beam weapon is already cooling, and a crowd is already scattering, and he is already dead, and he has always known he would be. So it goes.

There was a boy. There is a boy. He is born in a small industrial town and grows into a weak, peculiar child, and his father throws him into the deep end of a pool to teach him to swim, and he sinks to the bottom, and the water holds him like a promise. He does not drown. He comes up. The light breaks over his face. The light breaks over his face again years later when the prisoners in the meat locker come up to find the great city gone, destroyed by fire in one night, and the air above it is the colour of a bruise. So it goes.

He is lost behind the lines with a scout who beats him for wanting to be left to die. The pair are captured. The scout dies of gangrene on the prison train, blaming him with his last breath, and the breath is still out there somewhere, still blaming, still warm. He is held in a camp beside enemy officers who have been drawing double rations for years through a clerical error. He is sent on to a great city and housed with other prisoners in a disused abattoir. The prisoners are made to dig bodies out of the cellars until one of the diggers dies of the dry heaves. A fellow prisoner promises to have him killed one day on the dead scout's account. The promise is still standing. It has always been standing.

He is conscripted as a chaplain's assistant and shipped overseas with no training worth the name. The aliens explain that every moment exists at once and that free will is an idea peculiar to his own planet. He is taken by them and kept in a zoo on their planet with a film actress, and the actress is still there, still golden, still unattainable, and the zoo is still clean and well-lit. He goes on a radio talk show and tries to tell the world about the aliens and the fourth dimension. His daughter decides he is senile and takes his affairs out of his hands. She has always been deciding this. The paperwork is already signed.

He comes home, collapses, and is hospitalised, where another patient introduces him to a hack science fiction writer. He marries the daughter of the man who owns the optometry school and becomes rich. He survives an air crash in the mountains, and his wife dies of exhaust fumes driving to the hospital, and the exhaust is still curling from the tailpipe, and she is still turning the key, and she is already gone. So it goes.

He is shot dead by a beam weapon after addressing a crowd, exactly as he has always known he would be. The crowd is already gathering. The beam weapon is already aimed. He is already speaking, and the words are already leaving him, and the light is already breaking over his face, and the water is already closing over his head, and the city is already burning, and the prisoners are already climbing out of the meat locker into ash and silence, and the scout is already dying on the train, already blaming him, and the boy is already being born in a small industrial town, weak and peculiar, and the pool is already full, and the bottom is already there, waiting, and he is already sinking toward it, and he has always been sinking, and the moment exists at once, all of it, all at once, and there is no before and no after, only the blue light and the silence and the water holding him like a promise that cannot be kept or broken because it was never made, because there is no one to make it, because free will is an idea peculiar to his own planet, and he is not on his own planet anymore. So it goes.

On a business flight I sat next to a soap salesman named Rex Marrow. He talked with his hands, handed me a card, and I pocketed it without thinking. That night my flat and every piece of catalogue furniture in it were destroyed in an explosion. I called Rex from the rubble. He drove me to a derelict house at the edge of the industrial district and told me I could stay.

Outside a bar that first week, Rex asked me to hit him as hard as I could. I did. He hit me back. We beat each other bloody in the car park until we were both laughing, sitting in the gravel with split lips. What started as two men brawling hardened into a weekly basement club with its own rules—no shoes, no shirts, no talking about it outside—and it pulled in more and more members every week.

Rex burned my hand with lye one night, pressing the chemical into my skin and holding me there while I screamed, refusing to let me retreat into the meditation I used to survive the pain. "This is your life," he said. "Stay in it."

Ada overdosed. Rex brought her back to the derelict house and the two of them began a loud affair I could not stand, hearing them through the wall every night. Meanwhile Rex was rendering fat stolen from a cosmetic surgery clinic into soap and selling it back to the department stores at eighty dollars a bar. I blackmailed my employer into paying me to stay away, using my own beaten face as the evidence. The cheques arrived monthly.

Then Rex turned the club into something else. He called it Havoc. He filled the house with shaven recruits who took orders, who vandalised corporate property, who stood at attention when he entered a room. One night he steered the car into oncoming traffic, let it roll, and then he was gone.

A member named Ogden was shot dead on an operation, and I started trying to shut the whole thing down. Travelling city to city, I found identical clubs everywhere and men who greeted me as Rex Marrow. In a rented room I stood in front of a mirror for a long time and worked it out: he and I were the same person. Rex had been acting while I slept. I called Ada. She confirmed it. She had been sleeping with me, not with a separate man.

I discovered that Havoc had mined the towers of the debt-record companies. I went to defuse the charges. Rex beat me down a stairwell in one of the towers, and I put a gun in my own mouth and shot myself through the cheek to kill him.

The shaven recruits delivered Ada to the tower. She found me bleeding on the floor and took my hand. We stood at the window and the buildings came down, and the glass shook, and she squeezed my fingers, and I squeezed back.
